newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian Islamist criticises PM's re-appointment.
newsitem.headline: Algerian Islamist criticises PM's re-appointment.

text.p: Algerian Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah, whose party won the second highest number of seats in the June general election, criticised President Liamine Zeroual for renaming the prime minister without consulting opposition leaders.

"It is unfortunate that the appointment of the head of the government was carried out without our having been consulted. This shows some policymakers still have a single-ruling-party mind," said Nahnah, head of the Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS).

Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, who was reappointed by Zeroual last week, was still trying to win backing for his government line-up. His party, the pro-government National Democratic Rally (RND), won 155 seats but needs the support of other political groups to have a majority in the 380-seat house.

Nahnah, who won one third of the vote in a 1995 presidential poll in which Zeroual scored an overwhelming victory, made his remarks in an interview published on Tuesday in Algeria's Liberte newspaper.

The MPS leader said Zeroual should have consulted opposition party leaders particularly as Algeria was experiencing rapid and deep changes, crowned by the election of a pluralist lower house in which 10 political parties are represented.

Nahnah said his party, which won 69 seats, was not in hurry to forge alliances in the parliament but he hailed the outcome of the election which, he said, underlined the weak support for hardline anti-Islamists among ordinary Algerians.

"The presence of the (Islamist) Nahda, with this number (of 34) seats, alongside the FLN (National Liberation Front) constitutes for us evidence that Algeria has chosen an Islamic- Nationalist pro-democracy direction," he said.
Algeria's National Assembly will resume meeting on Tuesday to try to elect a speaker amid bargaining between the political groups.
Ouyahia, who was elected as an RND candidate and who is a leading figure in the party, is credited with good economic performance since he took over the cabinet in January 1996.

But his reforms to pull the once centrally commanded economy into a free market have upset many of the country's 29 million people. Many Algerian commentators say he also has an autocratic manner which deters other possible alliance partners.
